specialist_findings.claim: The pure-core / IO-adapter split is architecturally sound and consistent with the existing module boundary (statusline-session-shape.ts pure; statusline-identity.ts adapter). WS1/WS2/WS3 being IO-free with a single thin adapter in WS4 is the right structural choice for a constantly-ticking statusline.

The plan correctly identifies session-owned state (solo floor) as the authoritative source and shared substrate as the publication medium only. This reversal from substrate-as-source to session-as-source directly addresses the substrate-pointer failure pattern documented in the comms research.

WS2 names a specific dedup reconciliation: current code deduplicates on (name, session_id_prefix) at statusline-session-shape.ts:164-166, but the plan mandates the full (agent_name, id) tuple per PDR-076a. This is a named inconsistency with a fix deferred to WS2 execution. It is the right call to flag and defer, but the adapter boundary between the published-state reader and the dedup logic is not yet specified — the plan should name where the dedup lives (core or adapter) so the IO-free guarantee is not accidentally broken.

The bounded-source set (claims, comms-heartbeats, ArcAngel-rosters) forms a sufficient union for active-agent identity as argued, but the plan defers conversations/ and sidebars/ pending a roster contract. The architecture risk is that a future re-admission of those sources would require schema changes to the IO adapter boundary defined in WS4. A note that the adapter interface should expose a typed source-registry (not a hardcoded glob list) would protect against closed-shape erosion at that seam.

WS4 replaces resolveSessionShape but the plan does not specify whether the replacement is an in-place refactor of the same module or a new module that the adapter calls. Given the plan names statusline-session-shape.ts (pure), statusline-identity.ts (adapter), statusline-render.ts, and statusline-indicators.ts as co-updated files, the module graph after WS4 is underspecified. A one-sentence module-graph statement in WS4 (which module owns the session-state model, which owns the team-state derivation) would prevent accidental IO leakage into the pure layer during execution.

The owner_presence opinion is modelled as a closed union (present-and-engaged / away / unknown-about-the-owner) but WS1 defers the signal derivation to a later discovery question. The architecture risk is that the IO adapter (WS4) will need to produce a value for this field with no specified signal source, which means it will effectively always emit the unknown enum variant. If that variant is treated downstream as semantically different from a missing field, the closed union creates a false precision. The plan should explicitly state that the adapter emits the unknown variant as the default and that the acceptance criteria for WS1 confirm this is not treated as an error state.

The plan correctly scopes out new coordination machinery and CLIs/watchers/hooks (Non-goals), but it does not state a boundary on publication: a session publishes its state, but the plan does not specify what write surface is used, who initiates the write, or the write frequency. For the pure-core guarantee to hold through WS4 wiring, the publication path (which module calls the write, when) needs to be named — otherwise the architecture boundary between session-state ownership and substrate publication is implicit.

specialist_findings.claim: The manifest embeds a concrete model name ('gpt-5.4-xhigh') for Cursor at line 49. Hard-coded model identifiers in a canonical manifest are a maintenance liability: Cursor's model naming is vendor-controlled and will drift independently of the manifest. The plan's own 'Drift between canonical and adapter — Impossible' claim (line 95) is undermined if the manifest itself becomes a drift surface for model names.

The Turbo task definition (lines 73–80) lists '.claude/rules/**' as an output. Rules under .claude/rules/ are currently also canonical-authored artefacts (e.g. invoke-*.md). Treating them as build outputs while they may also be hand-edited creates a write-conflict: a developer editing a rule by hand and then running generate:adapters will have their edit silently overwritten. The plan declares rules as generated (line 66) but does not resolve the hand-edit vs generated conflict beyond a header comment.

The generation script is proposed as 'scripts/generate-adapters.mjs (or .ts)' (line 59). The repo rule feedback_no_workspace_to_root_scripts.md requires workspace scripts to be TypeScript with no exceptions; scripts/ is the no-checks zone. Placing a non-trivial manifest-driven generator in scripts/ (no-checks zone) rather than a workspace package means it escapes type checking, lint, and test coverage permanently, contrary to the plan's goal of a correctness guarantee.

The plan's promotion trigger (lines 143–148) has no concrete metric for 'demonstrably unsustainable' and the plan itself concedes this threshold 'is arguably already the case'. Leaving promotion criteria vague means the plan can sit in future/ indefinitely without a forced decision. A concrete count or a taxonomy-rename date would make this actionable.

The plan correctly identifies sequencing: this plan should precede the taxonomy rename (ADR-135) and should follow the portability remediation plan hardening the three-layer contract (lines 119–130). The dependency graph is explicit and consistent with the estate relationships described.

The complementary lane separation between internally-authored canonical artefacts (this plan) and externally-authored skill pack ingestion (canonical-first-skill-pack-ingestion-tooling.plan.md) is architecturally clean and correctly noted as sharing the same Layer-2 output directories and validator surface (lines 134–140).
